title: Minutes of the SONIA Stakeholder Advisory Group - 25 September 2026
body:
Minutes of the SONIA Stakeholder Advisory Group - 25 September 2026 | Bank of England – the UK's central bank Our use of cookies We use necessary cookies to make our site work. We’d also like to use some non-essential cookies (including third-party cookies) to help us improve the site. By clicking ‘Accept recommended settings’ on this banner, you accept our use of analytics cookies.   For more information on how these cookies work please see our Cookie policy . Accept recommended cookies Proceed with necessary cookies only Skip to main content Minutes of the SONIA Stakeholder Advisory Group - 25 September 2026 The SONIA Stakeholder Advisory Group supports the Bank’s administration of SONIA by providing advice and technical input to the Bank and the SONIA Oversight Committee Published on  
        15 October 2026 Date: 25 September 2026 Minutes Welcome / introductions The Chair welcomed the Group and those present as part of the SSAG observers’ programme and the Bank’s Step Into My Shoes observer programme. Diversity, Equity & Inclusion The Group discussed talent stream opportunities in place across firms, which provide engagement and support from school students through to early career employees.  Firms continue to utilise recruitment strategies aimed at providing a diverse workforce and creating value by bringing perspectives, knowledge and experiences from a diverse range of backgrounds. Retrospective review of market conditions The unsecured overnight market remained stable, with daily volumes of around £55 billion and the spread to Bank rate fluctuating close to 1.9 basis points.  Money-market funds had experienced collective inflows of approximately £15 billion since the start of the year and had increased allocation to the overnight tenor following changes in liquidity guidance and increased geopolitical tensions.  This further supported activity in short-dated markets, while repo-market volatility and month-end spikes were lower than in the previous year. Bank of England information gathering powers The Bank of England and His Majesty’s Treasury are reviewing the statutory powers used to collect sterling money market information. This review seeks to ensure the Bank’s data collection powers are sufficient to maintain strong coverage and visibility of Sterling Money Market activity including as markets evolve, for example should there be changes in market structure, regulation, infrastructure or booking locations. The Bank may seek to collect data on material Sterling Money Market activity in group entities to preserve sufficient coverage for SONIA if necessary, in future. Potential implications for SONIA of extending RTGS settlement hours The Bank of England consulted over the summer on its longer-term ambition to move RTGS and CHAPS settlement towards a near 24-hour, seven-day mode ( Extending RTGS and CHAPS settlement hours CP ) .  The Bank is reviewing feedback and intends to return to industry in the first quarter of 2027 with themes emerging from consultation responses and next steps. The Group discussed how longer settlement hours could affect SONIA’s definition, publication time, reporting, and operational processes. The Bank is continuing analysis on the impact of the proposed extended hours scenarios. Under one possible scenario, CHAPS settlement could close at 18:00, with the following day’s settlement starting at 20:00 – meaning between 20:00 and 00:00 there would be a discrepancy between the value date recorded in CHAPS, and calendar date. The Group discussed how market participants could eventually establish timestamp-based conventions.  Firms may delay or accelerate booking decisions to manage interest calculations. The Group also discussed potential impact of scenarios where CHAPS settlement closes later in the evening, considering SMMD reporting is required by 07:00 in order for the Bank to publish SONIA by 09:00. Participants noted that many reports are automated but the ability to resubmit or regenerate prior-day data were identified as particularly important. The Group indicated a strong preference to preserve the current SONIA publication time of 09:00. A later publication time could affect processing and fulfilment of products referencing SONIA. The proposed Sunday and, potentially in future, full-weekend CHAPS opening raised questions about whether weekend activity would be structurally different to volumes and rates traded on weekdays, and whether SONIA should be published for weekends or incorporate weekend activity into weekday data. ONS consultation on data release times The group discussed the Office for National Statistics consultation on release times for market-sensitive economic statistics. Release times had been moved to 07:00 during the Covid period, but the subsequent extension of trading hours for certain futures and gilt futures had changed the market context. The group noted that in July, ICE had extended trading hours for SONIA futures and gilt futures, both of which now open for trading at 01:00. Notwithstanding this, participants generally noted that data release times after 08:00 were preferable given deeper market liquidity after cash gilt and swap markets are open. That said, a 09:30 release was viewed as relatively late for pricing and trading decisions. Firms were encouraged to respond to the ONS consultation directly. Looking ahead Participants expected the year-end sterling cash market to be broadly stable, and likely to be driven by what happens in the repo market which was expected to be more stable than last year. Cross-currency basis dynamics were also expected to remain stable. Participants discussed the possibility that reserve drainage could increase reliance on Bank of England facilities and influence SONIA volumes and spread, and commercial-paper pricing. Others noted that the impact would depend not only on the aggregate quantity of reserves but also on where those reserves were held within the wider market. Liquidity in SONIA derivative markets The Bank’s Market Intelligence team presented developments in listed and over-the-counter SONIA markets following increased geopolitical volatility. SONIA futures and options recorded exceptionally high volumes in March, while open interest remained robust despite political uncertainty. More recent volatility had increased volumes again, but not to the record levels seen in March. ICE extended trading hours for SONIA futures and gilt futures had gone live on 6 July, which the group noted was enabling greater involvement from Asian, Middle Eastern, and United States-based clients. In SONIA swaps, turnover increased sharply during the March and April volatility before returning to more usual levels over the following three to four months. Amounts outstanding declined slightly, possibly reflecting the unwinding of positions established when markets expected lower rates.  Changes in hedge-fund positioning and the repricing of rate-cut expectations may also have contributed. AOB Members noted future topics for discussion, including a review of progress in the DMO T-bills market. title: The Nordics and NVIDIA Show What’s Possible When a Region Commits to Advanced Computing
body: The Nordics and NVIDIA Show What’s Possible When a Region Commits to Advanced Computing From building sovereign infrastructure and autonomous trucks to quantum-GPU supercomputing, Nordic countries are embracing and accelerating technological development. October 14, 2026 by Linda Malm 0 Comments Share Share This Article X Facebook LinkedIn Copy link Link copied! The Nordic countries have become the European leader in unicorn startup density, producing the most emerging companies valued at $1 billion or more per capita on the continent. Now, a new chapter for the region is unfolding as countries race to build one of Europe’s most consequential technology ecosystems. The many computing advancements already underway in the Nordics, combined with the opportunity that lies ahead, signal a region moving from ambition to application. NVIDIA’s Investments in the Nordics Over the past year, NVIDIA has invested in the technology ecosystem in the Nordics, including Sweden’s leading startups Lovable and Legora. Read All NVIDIA in Europe Announcements Lovable , a Stockholm-based startup, provides a software creation platform that enables anyone to build and run software using plain language. In collaboration with NVIDIA, Lovable is optimizing inference for open models and training its models using NVIDIA Dynamo software and Nemotron tools. Legora provides an agentic operating system for legal work, supporting lawyers in research, review and drafting across complex matters. Nordics Emerge as Infrastructure Hub The foundation for establishing the Nordics as a technology powerhouse is already being built and the region holds a structural advantage: abundant renewable energy, rigorous data governance and a research tradition that bridges academia and industry. The Nordics are one of Europe’s fastest growing hubs for infrastructure. AI clouds are expanding with a projected 1 gigawatts of capacity to be deployed across the region by the end of 2027. Among these cloud providers are Bitdeer, CoreWeave , Crusoe , Hyperstack, Nscale , Verda and Volta . In Sweden, a consortium anchored by Ericsson, AstraZeneca, Saab, SEB and Wallenberg Investments, with SKF as strategic partner, launched Sferical One — a shared supercomputer running on two NVIDIA DGX SuperPODs with 16 racks of NVIDIA DGX GB300 systems and 1,152 GPUs. The consortium will build services using NVIDIA Nemotron open models, which allow researchers to customize and deploy their models in a secure environment. Nordic-Built Intelligence Some of the Nordics’ leading technology companies are now building proprietary intelligence on NVIDIA infrastructure. Spotify , which personalizes music, podcasts and audiobooks for hundreds of millions of listeners, uses NVIDIA TensorRT-LLM inference software to run AI-powered podcast recommendations faster and cheaper at scale. The deployment is a case study in inference efficiency: delivering the same recommendations to a global audience at a lower cost per query. ABB Robotics developed RobotStudio HyperReality using NVIDIA Omniverse libraries to bridge the gap between robot simulations and real-world performance. By combining NVIDIA’s advanced simulation capabilities with ABB Robotics’ virtual controller, running the same firmware as its physical robots, the solution enables engineers to train, test and validate robots virtually, while using real-world data to continuously improve the digital model. According to ABB Robotics, the solution delivers up to 99% simulation accuracy and reduces commissioning time by up to 80%. Finnish telecom company Elisa is launching a beta of Moontalk AIRI, a real-time enterprise agentic assistant that retrieves information, captures insights and documents decisions during meetings and calls. Built on NVIDIA Nemotron open models and distributed infrastructure, it uses company data and low-latency networking to deliver fast, context-aware responses. Nordic Startups Scaling on NVIDIA Sweden’s startup ecosystem raised $2.8 billion in the first half of 2026 and is projected to reach $5 billion for the year. This next generation is building fast — and on open models. Stilta is reinventing how companies protect their inventions with intellectual property. The Stockholm-based startup is post-training NVIDIA Nemotron open models to scale patent analysis from a single patent to entire portfolios — work that was previously out of reach. Nemotron gives Stilta the language model accuracy for continuous portfolio monitoring at scale, across the thousands of patents that large industrial and technology companies hold. ConfidentialMind’s SampoTron , built on NVIDIA Nemotron-3-Embed, delivers more than 20% improvement in cross-lingual retrieval accuracy across English, Finnish and Swedish. Agaton , a platform that analyzes customer conversations in real time, is using NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Lightning to speed up Revenue Mining solution on live sales calls. By routing knowledge retrieval to Nemotron 3.5 Lightning, Agaton can cut response latency to deliver fast responses that inform customers’ buying decisions. Klang , a Swedish speech lab, fine-tuned the NVIDIA Parakeet v3 model to create Pianissimo — a Swedish transcription model that reduces errors by 75% while being 64x faster than the most accurate alternative. Built on over 50,000 hours of Swedish speech using the open source NVIDIA NeMo framework, the model is freely available on Hugging Face. Embedl , founded in Gothenburg and a member of the NVIDIA Inception program for cutting-edge startups, and Space Cargo Unlimited unveiled an onboard prototype that monitors protein crystallization, flags anomalies and recommends actions on a single NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX module, without continuous ground connectivity. Sweden AI Factory — one of Europe’s 19 EuroHPC-funded AI factories — announced a collaboration with NVIDIA to open its infrastructure and expertise to Inception startups and small- and medium-sized enterprises across industries, including life and material sciences, autonomous systems and gaming. Autonomous Machines on Nordic Roads and Factory Floors In Sweden, advanced computing is also powering vehicles on the road and machines in factories. Volvo Cars is combining its industry-leading vehicle safety systems and engineering expertise with NVIDIA Hyperion , Halos OS and Alpamayo Stack to enable future Volvo cars to safely navigate complex real-world environments from door to door. Autonomous freight company Einride is building its next-generation Einride Driver on NVIDIA Hyperion for autonomous freight trucks, using the NVIDIA Halos safety system and NVIDIA Cosmos open world models. Meanwhile, Toyota Material Handling Europe — the world’s leading forklift manufacturer — is bringing autonomous machines to factory floors. In a collaboration with NVIDIA and SoftServe, Toyota Material Handling Europe is adopting a simulation-first approach to autonomous material handling, cutting autonomous solution deployment time by up to 50% across its global engineering, manufacturing and innovation teams. Norrsken Foundation and NVIDIA are opening the Stockholm AI Lab, a physical hub for AI-native founders working on global challenges, set to open in 2027. Quantum Meets Accelerated Computing Finally, Swedish companies are advancing quantum research using NVIDIA’s quantum computing platform. Stockholm-based FirstQFM used NVIDIA accelerated computing to train a model that reduces the execution time of quantum processors by 33% without sacrificing performance. Validated on a QuantWare quantum processor unit, this model optimizes how the operations needed by quantum algorithms are turned into detailed hardware instructions, accounting for detailed updates on how the hardware is calibrated. Tune in to NVIDIA founder and CEO Jensen Huang’s GTC Berlin keynote on Wednesday, Oct. 21, at 11 a.m. CEST. The Stockholm-based startup is post-training NVIDIA Nemotron open models to scale patent analysis from a single patent to entire portfolios — work that was previously out of reach. Nemotron gives Stilta the language model accuracy for continuous portfolio monitoring at scale, across the thousands of patents that large industrial and technology companies hold. ConfidentialMind’s SampoTron , built on NVIDIA Nemotron-3-Embed, delivers more than 20% improvement in cross-lingual retrieval accuracy across English, Finnish and Swedish. Agaton , a platform that analyzes customer conversations in real time, is using NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Lightning to speed up Revenue Mining solution on live sales calls. By routing knowledge retrieval to Nemotron 3.5 Lightning, Agaton can cut response latency to deliver fast responses that inform customers’ buying decisions. Klang , a Swedish speech lab, fine-tuned the NVIDIA Parakeet v3 model to create Pianissimo — a Swedish transcription model that reduces errors by 75% while being 64x faster than the most accurate alternative. Built on over 50,000 hours of Swedish speech using the open source NVIDIA NeMo framework, the model is freely available on Hugging Face. Embedl , founded in Gothenburg and a member of the NVIDIA Inception program for cutting-edge startups, and Space Cargo Unlimited unveiled an onboard prototype that monitors protein crystallization, flags anomalies and recommends actions on a single NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX module, without continuous ground connectivity. Sweden AI Factory — one of Europe’s 19 EuroHPC-funded AI factories — announced a collaboration with NVIDIA to open its infrastructure and expertise to Inception startups and small- and medium-sized enterprises across industries, including life and material sciences, autonomous systems and gaming. Autonomous Machines on Nordic Roads and Factory Floors In Sweden, advanced computing is also powering vehicles on the road and machines in factories. Volvo Cars is combining its industry-leading vehicle safety systems and engineering expertise with NVIDIA Hyperion , Halos OS and Alpamayo Stack to enable future Volvo cars to safely navigate complex real-world environments from door to door. Autonomous freight company Einride is building its next-generation Einride Driver on NVIDIA Hyperion for autonomous freight trucks, using the NVIDIA Halos safety system and NVIDIA Cosmos open world models. Meanwhile, Toyota Material Handling Europe — the world’s leading forklift manufacturer — is bringing autonomous machines to factory floors. In a collaboration with NVIDIA and SoftServe, Toyota Material Handling Europe is adopting a simulation-first approach to autonomous material handling, cutting autonomous solution deployment time by up to 50% across its global engineering, manufacturing and innovation teams. Norrsken Foundation and NVIDIA are opening the Stockholm AI Lab, a physical hub for AI-native founders working on global challenges, set to open in 2027. Quantum Meets Accelerated Computing Finally, Swedish companies are advancing quantum research using NVIDIA’s quantum computing platform. Stockholm-based FirstQFM used NVIDIA accelerated computing to train a model that reduces the execution time of quantum processors by 33% without sacrificing performance. Validated on a QuantWare quantum processor unit, this model optimizes how the operations needed by quantum algorithms are turned into detailed hardware instructions, accounting for detailed updates on how the hardware is calibrated. Main Menu Toggle Button Sections Search Toggle Button Search Search Submit Button Submit Home News & Events Speeches Speech PDF October 14, 2026 Supervisory Modernization After Silicon Valley Bank Vice Chair for Supervision Michelle W. Bowman At the Bangkok Economic Festival, Reinventing Bretton Woods Committee, Bangkok, Thailand Share Watch Live Thank you for the invitation to join you today. It is good to be with you to discuss ensuring that the global financial system is positioned to adapt to the changing economic environment. 1 The pace of change has been brisk. Our financial system is evolving rapidly. Therefore, it is important that we periodically review our regulatory and supervisory frameworks to consider how to best keep pace with that evolution. Today, I will discuss three related aspects of supervisory modernization. First, I will describe some lessons learned from a newly released independent assessment of the failure of Silicon Valley Bank (SVB) about the importance of timely supervisory action. Second, I will discuss how the Federal Reserve is enhancing our supervisory effectiveness so that decisionmaking authority is clear and examiners are more accountable for taking timely action. And, third, I will describe how modernization can improve the work of supervision around the world, including under the direction of standard-setting bodies like the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (BCBS) and the Financial Stability Board (FSB). Independent Review of Silicon Valley Bank The failure of SVB in 2023 is a case study with critical lessons for bank supervisors at home and abroad. While prior reports on SVB provided important information, they were produced on an expedited basis with a limited scope and failed to comprehensively address important data related to the failure. As a result, these reports were incomplete and perpetuated a number of unreliable conclusions. That is why, earlier this year, I commissioned an independent review of the bank failure and the Federal Reserve's related supervision. The review closes prior gaps and corrects important misimpressions regarding SVB's failure. Its preliminary findings substantiate difficult but important critiques regarding Federal Reserve System supervision failures to act in a timely manner and to communicate actionable guidance to SVB. A central finding is that supervisors had information about SVB's major vulnerabilities many months before its failure but did not make appropriate use of it. Frontline examiners, risk and surveillance specialists, and Reserve Bank and Board staff knew about SVB's exposure to interest rate and liquidity risk at least as early as nine full months before the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation took the bank into receivership. The review concludes that long-standing uncertainty about decisionmaking authority and the lack of clear accountability impeded timely decisionmaking. The preliminary review also corrects earlier mischaracterization that social media was to blame for the run on SVB, and that the Fed's failure to act was caused by statutory tailoring or regulatory changes. 2 Instead, the report notes long-standing problems in supervisory accountability and decisionmaking as the most significant contributors to the failure to issue timely critical enforcement actions related to core risks. The Imperative of Timely Action While supervisory decisions must be grounded in evidence, legal authority, and judgment, the impact of supervisory decisions is only effective if delivered in time. When supervisors note vulnerabilities as they emerge, banks have more options and flexibility to course correct. At the point when weakness emerges, a bank can often gradually reduce exposure, strengthen its liquidity position, improve contingency planning, or raise capital under normal market conditions. But where supervisors perpetually delay communication or action—to continually wait for additional evidence, more concurrence, or another committee meeting—supervision bogs down and loses effectiveness. Timely and efficient action is key to successful supervisory outcomes. The review notes that supervisory attention at SVB often centered on process, procedure, governance, and controls rather than on mitigating the underlying interest rate and liquidity exposures. SVB had 54 matters requiring attention or immediate attention between 2019 and the time of its failure, yet none of those supervisory findings required the bank to address its core financial risks. In other words, a supervisory organization can be extremely busy and still fail to focus sufficiently on the risks that matter most. It can issue many findings, require firms to spend significant time and resources on remediation of less important process-related issues, and devote enormous resources to governance and process while failing to compel action on the vulnerabilities most capable of threatening the institution's existence. Supervisory Prioritization and Accountability A supervisory culture of timely action must also be paired with clear roles and responsibilities so that supervisors are empowered to act. The independent review describes uncertainty within the Federal Reserve System about decision rights and lack of accountability across the supervisory system. In our structure, different groups identified risks, many others were expected to concur, and yet no individual clearly owned the obligation to reach a decision and propel action. A modern supervisory organization needs clear answers to the basic questions of: who owns the decision to move forward? Who has authority to act? Who is accountable for ensuring that a material risk is addressed? And when different parts of the organization disagree, who is responsible to resolve that disagreement and keep pressing forward? Modern supervisory organizations increasingly rely on surveillance, specialist teams, and data analysis that allow us to identify patterns across institutions. Those capabilities are enormously valuable. But identifying a risk matters only if there is a clear path from information to judgment and from judgment to action. That is why we at the Federal Reserve System are considering ways to enhance our supervisory decisionmaking framework to ensure more direct allocation of responsibility, authority, and accountability between the Board and Reserve Bank staff; clear decision rights for examiners and supervisory leadership; and direct escalation channels from examination teams to senior supervision leadership. In the fall of 2025, the Board published a Statement of Supervisory Operating Principles clearly stating our expectations about how supervisors should conduct supervision. We have refined those principles, most recently to incorporate lessons learned from the independent review of the 2023 banking stress. Publishing these principles further improves supervisory transparency and accountability. They refocus supervisory efforts on what matters most: early identification of material risks, exercising sound supervisory judgment, and a broad range of supervisory tools to enable timely and proportionate action to address material risks before they threaten the safety and soundness of an institution or the stability of the financial system. International Implications and Proportionality The benefits of our supervisory modernization efforts are not limited to the Federal Reserve. They have implications far beyond the United States. Our reforms and the lessons learned from the independent review are equally applicable to supervisors around the world. As chair of the FSB's Standing Committee on Supervisory and Regulatory Cooperation, I have engaged many member jurisdictions to advance the FSB's regulatory and supervisory modernization agenda. The FSB's 2026 work program reflects that countries around the world are also evaluating whether regulatory and supervisory frameworks remain well suited for future financial systems. There are important common themes in that work. Modernization is not about doing less. It is about more effectively prioritizing the things that matter the most. This includes concentrating on material risks, appropriately tailoring supervisory intensity, periodically reconsidering processes that may have accumulated over time to ensure they are still fit for purpose, and providing clarity so that supervisors can reach decisions quickly enough to make a difference. Tailoring or proportionality does not mean weaker supervision. It means directing supervisory attention to the risks that are most material given the institution's size, complexity, activities, business model, interconnectedness, and potential impact on financial stability. A community bank engaged in conventional lending and deposit-taking does not require the same supervisory approach as a globally active institution engaged in complex trading and cross-border activities. The purpose of prioritization is to distinguish issues that are genuinely capable of threatening safety and soundness from matters that may warrant attention but do not present the same degree of financial risk. This distinction requires supervisory judgment. And judgment inevitably requires making choices. A supervisory organization that treats every issue as equally important will tend to devote substantial attention to matters that are easiest to document, measure, and track, leaving other risks that require synthesis, experience, and enhanced judgment to receive less attention than they deserve. The objective should not be to maximize the number of findings that are issued. It should be to identify the risks that matter most and address them while there is still time to alter the trajectory. International bodies, including the BCBS and the FSB, can help most in this supervisory modernization effort by focusing on their core mandates and by remaining evidence and data driven. They should prioritize work on areas that matter most—issues related to safety and soundness as well as financial stability. International Lessons Learned The independent review of SVB shows that international standard-setting bodies, including the BCBS and the FSB, relied unquestioningly on incomplete reports compiled quickly and shortly after the failure of SVB. The independent review found that both the BCBS and the FSB took language nearly verbatim from other reports published in the United States that were not based on complete or accurate information. The independent review determined that these reports from the BCBS and the FSB generally repeated existing claims by other reports rather than independently verifying the information or increasing the breadth of evidence offered in their support. As a result, the purported lessons learned put forth in the April 2023 report by then–Vice Chair Barr were initially used to justify additional regulatory work, including at the BCBS and the FSB. That work was inherently flawed because it was based on incomplete and faulty initial report findings, not a broader analysis like that provided by the independent review. Now, with the benefit of more comprehensive evidence and analysis, we can see that the international bodies' work based on prior results was not justified. The BCBS's mandate is to strengthen regulation and supervision practices worldwide with the purpose of enhancing financial stability. 3 Similarly, the FSB was established to coordinate and promote effective regulatory, supervisory, and other financial-sector policies in the interest of global financial stability. 4 To maintain their credibility, these institutions must redouble their focus on material risks—those that affect safety and soundness or financial stability—while eschewing less valuable work that misdirects resources toward less valuable priorities. These institutions must also seek to validate data and analysis that is relied upon for international standards and regulations. Simply accepting data and analysis without rigorous validation risks building international standards on flawed foundations, potentially undermining both the effectiveness of regulations and the credibility of these critical institutions. Refocusing action on issues of material harm will allow these institutions to remain true to their core mandates and serve a more valuable purpose in fostering supervisory modernization. Conclusion As we continue to modernize supervision and regulation at the Federal Reserve, and as we work with our international colleagues through the FSB and the BCBS on modernization, we must have the humility to continually reevaluate the effectiveness of our own supervisory processes. We should continue to assess how we make sure our supervisory efforts are keeping pace with a rapidly changing ecosystem. For instance, how do we organize our people to allocate authority and prioritize risks? How do we tailor supervisory intensity and equip our staff to quickly move from identifying a material vulnerability to taking appropriate action? The financial system will continue to evolve rapidly. Our supervisory institutions must evolve with it. A critical measure of whether that modernization succeeds will be whether supervisors are able to identify the risks that matter and act decisively at the point when their actions can have the greatest impact. Thank you. 1. The views expressed here are my own and are not necessarily those of my colleagues on the Federal Reserve Board or the Federal Open Market Committee. Return to text 2. title: Sullivan & Cromwell brings legal expertise into agreement review
body: October 15, 2026 Sullivan & Cromwell brings legal expertise into agreement review In collaboration with OpenAI, Sullivan & Cromwell developed Agreement Analyzer, an AI tool for identifying issues in a draft agreement. Contact sales Company size: Enterprise Region: North America Industry: Services Products: ChatGPT Loading… Share For lawyers at Sullivan & Cromwell, reviewing a draft agreement includes weighing its terms against relevant precedents, using approaches based on the Firm’s experience and being mindful of a client’s priorities. The firm’s Agreement Analyzer brings those inputs into a single review workflow, producing analysis and proposed changes that lawyers can inspect and refine. “I think AI will . . . allow lawyers to focus on the areas where their judgment is most important . . . so they can concentrate on the questions that are most critical for their clients.” —John Savva, Partner, Sullivan & Cromwell Bringing firm expertise into agreement review Though AI was initially used most for repetitive, administrative tasks like drafting email responses or checking calendars, Savva finds that recent improvements in AI models’ analytical capabilities have changed its usage. “Now, we’re seeing many more opportunities for use in challenging legal tasks such as deep analysis of complex agreements,” he says. Agreement Analyzer helps lawyers compare corresponding provisions across precedents and track how those provisions interact. Sullivan & Cromwell partner John Savva developed Agreement Analyzer as a single-user proof of concept built with Codex. He then collaborated with OpenAI on improving the quality of outputs, enhancing efficiency through parallel processing and transforming the application into a tool that could be used by multiple lawyers at the same time. Agreement Analyzer integrates Sullivan & Cromwell’s workflows, curated firm precedents, negotiating playbooks and ChatGPT Enterprise. After inputting a draft agreement into the tool, a lawyer can add their own selected precedents and a playbook with firm and client positions, as well as information on market practice. The tool performs multiple review cycles from different perspectives, synthesizes the outputs, helps identify potential issues and returns a memorandum and proposed tracked changes for a lawyer to review, adapt or reject. “It’s not about replacing lawyers. It’s about providing a tool for lawyers to do deeper analyses and find more authority and precedents to provide an even higher quality product for their clients.” —John Savva, Partner, Sullivan & Cromwell Making sources and uncertainty visible Savva emphasizes that what makes an AI tool’s output trustworthy is full transparency. “If an AI tool makes a claim about market practice, you need to be able to see the source of that information,” he says. Savva describes an application in which agents develop conclusions and other agents challenge them in an adversarial process. In a potential use case, specialized agents review the agreement in parallel for such things as market deviations and risk allocation, interactions between clauses, and ambiguities that could impact litigation. The results distinguish findings supported after challenge by other agents, dismissed findings, and unverified issues retained with qualifications. Lawyers can inspect the issues, their supporting explanations, and the relevant precedents, then decide which findings warrant changes in the final markup. What’s next Sullivan & Cromwell is continuing to explore tools shaped around specific legal tasks. For Savva, stronger analytical capabilities create an opportunity to support more of the research and writing process. Savva points to advances in reasoning capabilities with GPT‑6 Astra: “Astra’s really moved things forward in terms of the quality of the reasoning that’s available, and that has been the bottleneck in the past,” he says. Join the new era of work More than 1 million businesses around the world are achieving meaningful results with OpenAI.
